cf.title: Archive-fed logical decoding: pausing recovery on slot conflict

input.subject: Archive-fed logical decoding: pausing recovery on slot conflict

verdict_reasoning: The goal is plausible and a reviewer supports it, but the design is not settled. v2 admits that some pauses cannot resolve (replication-ondisk-1) and nothing bounds them (standards-compat-1). The per-slot question from message #1 is still open (standards-compat-3), and the proposal does not say how the wait inside redo handles reload and shutdown (prior-attempts-1). These are fixable, but the list needs to agree on them before code review.

brief.title: Pause standby recovery instead of invalidating logical slots on catalog conflict
brief.problem: A standby fed only by restore_command has no walreceiver, so it cannot send hot_standby_feedback to the primary. Catalog prune and B-tree delete records then conflict with the local logical slot's catalog_xmin, and the slot is invalidated, roughly 2 * autovacuum_naptime after creation. This blocks continuous CDC from a WAL archive without load on the primary.
brief.proposed_design: A new GUC, recovery_pause_on_logical_slot_conflict, makes ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot() pause recovery before it would invalidate a local logical slot. Recovery resumes automatically once normal logical decoding has advanced the slot's effective xmin horizons past the conflict, using the normal invalidation predicate. In v2 the startup process no longer changes slot horizons; pg_wal_replay_resume() lets the slot be invalidated and promotion ends the pause.
user_visible_surface: New GUC recovery_pause_on_logical_slot_conflict (boolean, PGC_SIGHUP, default off).
pg_wal_replay_resume() during a conflict pause now means "give up and invalidate the slot".
New recovery pause cause, visible through pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state() and one log line at pause start.
Synchronized slots are excluded from the protection.
author_claims: The catalog conflict is the only fundamental blocker for archive-fed logical decoding; wal_level and WAL removal are already operator knobs.
With the GUC off, the cost is one boolean early return.
The feature reuses the existing recovery pause machinery and adds no shared memory.
A TAP test and a WAL-G field test with pg_recvlogical show the slot survives with no gaps, while a GUC-off control standby loses its slot.
Consumers such as pg_recvlogical and Debezium should see ordinary standby decoding with occasional stalls.
brief.thread_state: Andrey posted v1, then v2 after self-review found v1's startup-process advance of catalog_xmin unsafe. Ajin Cherian likes the idea but asks for a maximum pause duration and repeated warnings, because a dead consumer would stall the standby forever.
unclear: The patch has no bound on pause length and no answer yet to Ajin's max-pause proposal.
The authors' own design questions are unanswered: per-slot option versus global GUC, and an out-of-band feedback channel versus pausing.
The material does not say how often a pause cannot be resolved because decoding cannot derive a recent enough horizon.
The effect on cascading standbys and on a standby that is also a failover target is not discussed.
No measurement of standby lag or pause frequency under realistic catalog churn is given.

prior_attempts.title: Use latch instead of pg_usleep for standby recovery conflicts
prior_attempts.quote: Calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() is actually dangerous I think, because it would reload the GUC context while replaying a record.
prior_attempts.reason: Review found that CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() does nothing in the startup process and that WL_LATCH_SET has no effect because MyLatch is never set there. Michael Paquier then judged that calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() would reload the GUC context in the middle of replaying a record. He concluded that all conflict code paths should use a latch, and returned the patch with feedback as time ran short.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P12 changed how an existing conflict wait sleeps. This proposal adds a new wait at the same place inside record replay, so P12's concern about reloading configuration in the middle of a record applies to it.

objections.title: Some pauses cannot resolve because of WAL ordering, and nothing bounds them
objections.failure_scenario: On the primary, a catalog row deleted by xid X is pruned on access soon after X commits, before the next xl_running_xacts is logged. The standby pauses before the prune record. Decoding can read only up to the replay position, so it never sees a running_xacts newer than X, and the standby waits until someone notices.
objections.argument: Message #2 and the docs say a pause may not be resolvable, but the patch does not say how often this happens or why. Decoding gets a new catalog_xmin candidate from xl_running_xacts records. Any running_xacts that would move the horizon past the prune horizon may sit after the pause LSN, where decoding cannot reach it. That would make the stall a regular event under catalog churn, and the auto-resume promise that message #1 makes depends on how often it happens.
objections.author_must_show: Under realistic catalog churn, what fraction of conflict pauses can decoding resolve from WAL already replayed, and what ends the others without an operator?

critic.reasoning: Decoding advances catalog_xmin only from xl_running_xacts records it has read, and a prune record can precede the first such record that passes its horizon. Message #2 admits unresolvable pauses but gives no frequency, and nothing ends them without an operator.

objections.title: Unbounded conflict wait departs from the max_standby_*_delay pattern
objections.failure_scenario: The pg_recvlogical process on an archive-fed standby crashes overnight. Recovery pauses at the next catalog prune record and stays paused, while cascading standbys and readers see data that keeps getting older. Monitoring that checks only for invalidated slots or walreceiver state reports nothing wrong.
objections.argument: Every existing recovery conflict wait in Postgres is bounded by max_standby_archive_delay or max_standby_streaming_delay, and waiting forever requires the explicit value -1. The proposal adds a conflict wait with no bound, controlled by an on/off boolean. Message #3 asks for a maximum pause duration and repeated warnings, and v2 gives no answer. If a delay setting is added later, the boolean stays behind as a second knob that cannot be removed.
objections.author_must_show: Why should this conflict wait be an unbounded boolean, when other recovery conflict waits use a delay setting where -1 means wait forever?

critic.reasoning: Existing recovery conflict waits take their limit from max_standby_archive_delay or max_standby_streaming_delay, and the proposal adds a boolean with no limit. Message #3 asks for a ceiling and the visible thread has no reply.

objections.title: Cluster-wide GUC for behaviour that slot properties already express
objections.failure_scenario: A standby serves as a failover target and also hosts a CDC slot and a test slot that someone left behind. With the GUC on, the abandoned test slot stalls replay for the whole standby. With the GUC off, the CDC slot is invalidated. No setting protects only the CDC slot.
objections.argument: Per-slot behaviour such as failover and two_phase is set as a slot property at creation. Here a server-wide GUC decides how every local logical slot reacts to conflicts. Message #1 asks the same question (item 2) and calls the GUC coarse, and v2 keeps the GUC without saying why. If a per-slot option is added later, the GUC becomes a lasting second interface.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a server-wide GUC preferable to a per-slot option, given that the thread itself raised the per-slot option and existing slot behaviours are set per slot?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 calls the cluster-wide GUC coarse and asks about a per-slot option, and v2 keeps the GUC without giving a reason. The abandoned test slot case is concrete, and no setting in the proposal protects only one slot.

objections.title: Unbounded wait inside record replay versus startup interrupt handling
objections.failure_scenario: A consumer dies and recovery pauses inside ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot() for hours. The operator sets recovery_pause_on_logical_slot_conflict = off and reloads, or runs pg_ctl stop. Either the startup process never handles the SIGHUP or shutdown request, or it handles it while a record is half replayed.
objections.argument: Existing recovery pauses happen between records in the main loop, and other conflict waits inside redo are bounded by max_standby_*_delay. This pause sits inside a record's redo and has no bound (message #3). In [P12], the recorded reason was that calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() there would reload the GUC context while a record is being replayed. v1-0001 lists only ConfirmRecoveryPaused() and CheckForStandbyTrigger() for the wait loop, and does not say how config reload and shutdown are handled.
objections.author_must_show: How does the conflict wait handle SIGHUP and shutdown requests during a long pause, and why is that safe in the middle of replaying a record?

precedents.title: Use latch instead of pg_usleep for standby recovery conflicts

critic.reasoning: The patch prose names only ConfirmRecoveryPaused() and CheckForStandbyTrigger() for the wait loop, and does not say how reload or shutdown is handled. One correction: existing conflict waits are also unbounded when max_standby_*_delay is -1, so [P12] supports the reload concern only.

objections.title: Primary-side placeholder slot can already hold catalog_xmin without streaming
objections.failure_scenario: An operator who can run one SQL connection to the primary keeps a logical slot there. A small job advances it to the standby slot's restart_lsn, so the primary never prunes catalog rows the standby still needs. With this setup the core GUC adds nothing, and the stalls it causes on the archive-fed standby can be avoided.
objections.argument: Message #1, question 1, names an out-of-band channel that publishes the standby's catalog_xmin back to the primary as a possible long-term answer. Postgres can already build that channel with pg_create_logical_replication_slot and pg_replication_slot_advance on the primary. The author's goal is no load on, and no dependency on, the primary. That makes the existing way less convenient, because it keeps WAL on the primary and needs a connection, but it does not make it impossible. A committer would likely ask which users truly cannot open any connection to the primary.
objections.author_must_show: Which deployments cannot run a primary-side logical slot advanced by an external job, and why is a recovery pause on the standby better for them?

critic.reasoning: A logical slot on the primary, advanced by an external job, can hold catalog_xmin back without a streaming standby. The proposal states the goal of no load on the primary but does not show which deployments cannot open a connection to it.

other_surviving.title: Demand rests on one team's use case, with no outside users shown
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A committer adds a GUC and a new recovery pause cause, and then owns them. The only known users are on a dedicated decoding replica fed by restore_command, a setup that may be rare. If the group stays small, every later change to recovery conflict handling must keep this path working for a few installations.
other_surviving.argument: The only evidence of demand is the authors' own WAL-G field test (message #1) and one reviewer who likes the idea (message #3). No -general or -bugs reports, Debezium users or other operators are cited. Message #1 also narrows the audience to dedicated decoding replicas, because the pause is "bad for one that is also an HA target". The obvious alternative is a streaming standby with hot_standby_feedback, which costs only some catalog bloat on the primary, and the thread gives no numbers showing that this cost is a real problem.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which operators run archive-only standbys for CDC today, and what measured primary-side cost makes a hot_standby_feedback streaming standby unacceptable for them?

critic.reasoning: The visible thread shows the authors' WAL-G field test and one supportive reviewer, with no outside reports. It gives no measured primary-side cost for the streaming standby with hot_standby_feedback, so this is a show-demand point.

refuted.title: pg_wal_replay_resume() gains a destructive meaning existing tools cannot see
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator's runbook or an HA script calls pg_wal_replay_resume() whenever pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state() reports 'paused', for example after a recovery_target pause. On a standby with this GUC on, that same call now invalidates the CDC slot. The loss shows up only when the consumer reconnects and gets an error.
refuted.argument: Today pg_wal_replay_resume() only resumes replay and never destroys state. The proposal makes it mean "give up and invalidate the slot" when the pause comes from a slot conflict. The material says the cause is visible in pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state() and in one log line, but it does not say which new value existing clients will see or how a script tells the two cases apart.
refuted.author_must_show: What exact value does pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state() return during a conflict pause, and how do existing tools that call pg_wal_replay_resume() avoid invalidating the slot by mistake?

critic.reasoning: The documentation hunk says an explicit resume keeps the default invalidation, which is what happens today without the GUC. A script that resumes every pause already ends recovery at a recovery_target pause, so pg_wal_replay_resume() is not free of lasting effects today.

refuted.title: Automatic pause also stalls cascading standbys and primaries using remote_apply
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator enables the GUC on a standby that has a walreceiver and is listed in synchronous_standby_names with synchronous_commit = remote_apply. A consumer lags, replay pauses, and commits on the primary block. Cascading standbys fed by this standby also stop advancing, and nobody is told why.
refuted.argument: The GUC applies to any standby, not only archive-fed ones. A manual pg_wal_replay_pause() has the same effect, but in that case an operator chose it. Here a slow or dead logical consumer triggers it with no ceiling, which message #3 raised and the thread has not answered. Message #1 also notes the conflict with standbys that are failover targets, and v2 has no guard for any of these cases.
refuted.author_must_show: Should the pause be limited to standbys with no walreceiver and no downstream, or bounded in time, and how does v2 protect remote_apply primaries and cascading standbys?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which asks for the same time limit. The remote_apply and cascading stalls already occur when an operator sets max_standby_streaming_delay = -1, and here too the cost follows an explicit setting.

refuted.title: Any REPLICATION user can halt standby replay with an idle slot
refuted.failure_scenario: An admin enables the GUC for one CDC slot. A second role with REPLICATION, such as a backup or monitoring account, creates a logical slot on the same standby and never consumes it. Replay stops at the next catalog prune record and stays stopped until someone notices the frozen read-only queries or lag.
refuted.argument: The GUC is cluster-wide and protects every non-synchronized local logical slot, so the admin's opt-in hands every slot holder the power to stop replay. Without the GUC, an idle slot only loses itself and replay goes on. Message #1 (question 2) offers a per-slot opt-in, but v2 keeps the global GUC. Postgres already bounds slot harm with settings such as max_slot_wal_keep_size, and the patch adds no bound on pause length (message #3).
refuted.author_must_show: How does an administrator limit the pause power to the one slot they trust, so another REPLICATION role cannot stop replay for all standby users?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-3, which covers the per-slot opt-in. The privilege angle adds little, because with max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 any role that can run a query can already stall replay.

refuted.title: Cluster-wide GUC stalls all replay for one slot's benefit
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator enables the GUC on a standby that serves read queries and feeds a cascading replica, and one slow or idle logical consumer pauses replay. Readers and the cascaded standby fall behind. Nothing in the slot list shows which slot caused it.
refuted.argument: Message #1 itself calls a global GUC that stalls all replay "coarse" and asks whether a per-slot option is cleaner, but v2 in message #2 keeps the global GUC without answering. Every user of the standby bears the cost, and only the decoding consumer gains from it. A GUC, once released, has to stay compatible for years. Choosing the wrong grain now leaves the project with both a GUC and a later slot option.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is a server-wide GUC preferable to a per-slot option, given that one slot can hold back every reader and cascaded standby?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-3, which makes the same per-slot argument with a more concrete scenario.

refuted.title: Unbounded pause will likely need more knobs to be safe
refuted.failure_scenario: A pg_recvlogical consumer crashes overnight, and recovery pauses with no end. Only one log line marks the start, so the stall is found when someone notices stale data. A later fix then adds a timeout GUC and a repeated-warning interval on top.
refuted.argument: Message #3 asks for a maximum pause duration and repeated warnings, and the material has no reply to that. If those are added, one feature becomes two or three GUCs and a pause cause with timer semantics. If ten features each add knobs like this in a release, the recovery configuration grows hard to reason about. The design should settle its bounded form before the first GUC lands, so the interface is not changed after release.
refuted.author_must_show: What is the full, bounded interface, including timeout and repeated warnings, and can it stay a single setting or a slot property?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which already says that a later delay setting would leave the boolean behind as a second knob.

refuted.title: New wait inside record replay needs a stated rule for interrupts
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator turns recovery_pause_on_logical_slot_conflict off and reloads the configuration to end a long pause. The startup process is waiting inside ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot() for the current record. The reload is either ignored until a manual resume, or the configuration changes in the middle of replaying a record.
refuted.argument: The GUC is PGC_SIGHUP, and the wait loop runs on the WAL apply path, outside recoveryPausesHere(), as the v1-0001 commit message describes. In [P12], a committer judged that calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() there could reload the GUC context while a record is being replayed. The proposal does not say which of the two behaviours it picks. Later changes to startup interrupt handling would also have to keep this second wait point in mind.
refuted.author_must_show: How does the conflict wait handle SIGHUP and other startup interrupts, and why is that safe in the middle of replaying a record?

precedents.title: Use latch instead of pg_usleep for standby recovery conflicts

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1, which covers both the reload and the shutdown case for the same wait loop.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a wait inside ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot() that pauses replay before a logical slot is invalidated.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds recovery_pause_on_logical_slot_conflict, a PGC_SIGHUP boolean that is off by default.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: With the GUC on, any role that owns an idle local logical slot can hold back replay for the whole standby.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A second pause point inside record replay and a new pause cause must be kept working through later changes to recovery.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The check runs on the replay path for snapshot conflicts; message #1 says the cost with the GUC off is one boolean test.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #1 asks whether an out-of-band feedback channel or a separate decoding-from-archive tool is the better layer.

questions: Under realistic catalog churn, what fraction of conflict pauses can decoding resolve from WAL already replayed, and what ends the others without an operator?
Will the pause get a time limit as message #3 asks, and if so, why not a delay setting where -1 means wait forever, like max_standby_archive_delay?
Why is a server-wide GUC preferable to a per-slot option, given that an abandoned slot can stall replay for the slot the operator wants to protect?
How does the conflict wait handle SIGHUP and shutdown requests during a long pause, and why is that safe in the middle of replaying a record?
Which deployments cannot keep a logical slot on the primary advanced by an external job, and why is a recovery pause on the standby better for them?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the startup process, recovery conflict handling and logical slot invalidation on standbys. The visible thread shows none taking part in that role.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new GUC, a new pause cause and a second wait point inside redo. All three must stay correct through later changes to recovery pause and slot invalidation, for as long as the GUC exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 after a self-review that found a safety problem in v1. The visible thread has no reply to message #3, and the entry has needed a rebase since 2026-09-25.

priority.reason: Message #1 limits the use to dedicated decoding standbys fed by restore_command, and shows demand only from the authors' own field test. The patch is small but changes the startup process and slot invalidation, and the pause bound and per-slot questions are open.

provisional_note: Without the code, the review could not check how the wait loop handles interrupts, or whether the pause and auto-resume are free of races with slot invalidation and concurrent decoding. It also could not check the claim of one boolean test with the GUC off.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reuse Workers and Replication Slots during Logical Replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a tablesync worker, after it finishes one table, pick up the next table in init state and sync it, keeping its replication slot. This removes the cost of starting a new worker and creating and dropping a slot for each table, which matters most for many empty or small tables.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks by reviewers showed regressions in some settings, and the v28 design #2 results were up to about twice as slow as HEAD and varied widely between runs. The patch also no longer applied to HEAD. Amit Kapila proposed Returned with feedback because the regressions still needed analysis, and vignesh C asked for a new entry with a fix for the regression.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
IIRC, there were some regressions observed with this patch. So, one
needs to analyze those as well.

precedents_retrieved.title: Minimal logical decoding on standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch allows logical decoding on a hot standby. It adds a catalog-table flag to existing WAL records so the standby can detect snapshot conflicts with logical slots, and it drops conflicting slots, including when wal_level on the primary drops below logical.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why the entry was withdrawn. The last messages show the patch set needing repeated rebases and its TAP tests failing intermittently: Rahila Syed reported 018_standby_logical_decoding_xmins.pl failures, and Alvaro Herrera found 019_standby_logical_decoding_conflicts.pl timing out after a rebase in March 2020. No later reply from the author is shown.

precedents_retrieved.title: Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
Reverted commit(s): Track conflict_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Till now, the reason for replication slot invalidation is not tracked
directly in pg_replication_slots. A recent commit 007693f2a3 added
'conflict_reason' to show the reasons for slot conflict/invalidation, but
only for logical slots.

This commit adds a new column 'invalidation_reason' to show invalidation
reasons for both physical and logical slots. And, this commit also turns
'conflict_reason' text column to 'conflicting' boolean column (effectively
reverting commit 007693f2a3). The 'conflicting' column is true for
invalidation reasons 'rows_removed' and 'wal_level_insufficient' because
those make the slot conflict with recovery. When 'conflicting' is true,
one can now look at the new 'invalidation_reason' column for the reason
for the logical slot's conflict with recovery.

The new 'invalidation_reason' column will also be useful to track other
invalidation reasons in the future commit.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix cancelled queries when hot_standby_feedback = on
precedents_retrieved.summary: With hot_standby_feedback = on, standby queries still get cancelled when vacuum truncates a heap on the primary, because the AccessExclusiveLock taken for truncation is replayed on the standby. The final patch adds a new lock level, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE LOCAL, that vacuum uses for heap truncation and that is not WAL-logged, so standby queries must tolerate concurrent truncation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane showed that letting scans run during truncation leaves a race: concurrent scans can load to-be-truncated pages back into shared buffers before ftruncate, and reading past EOF on a standby can extend the relation. Alexander Korotkov agreed the patch had to be revised and sketched a new truncation design, but Robert Haas called it fragile and doubted it prevents stale buffers from being taken as valid. No new version followed, the existing patch failed initdb, and the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: If we ever have valid-looking buffers in shared_buffers after the corresponding data has been truncated away on disk, we've got to make sure that nobody ever confuses one of them with an actually-valid buffer.

precedents_retrieved.title: Replica sends an incorrect epoch in its hot standby feedback to the Master
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a bug in Postgres 9.6, 10 and 11 where a replica's nextXid can move backward during WAL replay in RecordKnownAssignedTransactionIds, so hot standby feedback carries a wrong epoch and the master ignores the replica's xmin. The one-line fix advances nextXid only when the new value is higher, as similar code elsewhere does.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The withdrawal was not a rejection of the fix. The author registered the patch in the commitfest more than once, and David Steele marked the duplicate entries 2462 and 2463 as withdrawn. The visible messages show no objection, and Thomas Munro agreed the nextXid assignment looked wrong.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I have marked the duplicate entries 2462 and 2463 as withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Don't ignore recovery conflict interrupt on blocked writing
precedents_retrieved.summary: On a standby, a backend blocked writing results to a stuck or dead client ignores interrupts, so its buffer pin can block WAL replay until the TCP retransmission timeout, which can be about 15 minutes. The patch makes ProcessClientWriteInterrupt() handle recovery conflict interrupts during a blocked write and terminate the session, with a new Perl module for raw protocol tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund found that the patch did not promote the ERROR to FATAL, so the session was not really terminated. He also showed that the backend often reaches ProcessClientWriteInterrupt() with interrupts held, for example while sending an error message, and then the conflict is never resolved. The author posted a reworked approach on 2025-01-21. No reply follows in the visible messages, and they do not say why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Unfortunately I suspect that this means any protection we'd get from this version of the patch is rather incomplete - if the recovery conflict is triggered while not blocked, we'll ERROR out and report the message with interrupts held.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This part of the test was included originally in 4e87c48, but got
reverted as of f9c1b8d because of timing issues in the test, where,
after more analysis, we found that the standbys may not have recovered
from the archives all the segments needed by the test.  This stabilizes
the test by making sure that standbys replay up to the position returned
by pg_switch_wal(), meaning that all segments are recovered before the
manual checkpoint that tests WAL segment recycling and its interactions
with archive status files.

precedents_retrieved.title: Minimal logical decoding on standbys
precedents_retrieved.authors: Andres Freund (andresfreund), Craig Ringer (ringerc), Amit Khandekar (amitdkhan), Ibrar Ahmed (ibrar)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch allows logical decoding on a physical standby, with catalog-row conflicts on the standby detected from the existing snapshot-conflict WAL records, which gain a flag marking catalog tables. It replaces an earlier design that periodically logged the primary's catalog xmin horizon, and leaves hot_standby_feedback optional.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry died of inactivity. In March 2020 Alvaro Herrera rebased the patch, and its new conflict test then timed out and stopped the test run. No updated version followed, so after six months without updates Michael Paquier returned it with feedback, noting that the patch no longer applied.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use latch instead of pg_usleep for standby recovery conflicts
precedents_retrieved.summary: Simon Riggs added a CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() call to the standby's wait for recovery conflict resolution, and Michael Paquier then proposed a deeper fix for HEAD. That fix replaces the pg_usleep() in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithVirtualXIDs(), which can sleep up to 1s, with WaitLatch() and a new wait event.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Review found that CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() does nothing in the startup process and that WL_LATCH_SET has no effect because MyLatch is never set there. Michael Paquier then judged that calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() would reload the GUC context in the middle of replaying a record. He concluded that all conflict code paths should use a latch, and returned the patch with feedback as time ran short.

roaster_notes.note: The logical-decoding-on-standby entries ([P2], [P3], [P11], [P13]) built the base feature this proposal extends. They died of inactivity and failing tests, and those reasons do not apply here, so they are not listed.
No pg_dump, catalog or SQL-syntax concerns: the proposal adds only a GUC and changes recovery-pause semantics.
v2 no longer writes slot horizons or flushes slots from the startup process, so the crash-safety concern from v1 no longer applies. There is no new WAL record, catalog or on-disk format.
The feature adds no new SQL-visible data, no change to authentication and no new path for running user code as a privileged role. The only exposure is the replay stall that slot owners can now cause.
Objections were found from the maintenance and fit angle.
One objection from this angle. I know of no contrib module or extension that makes archive-fed logical decoding survive catalog conflicts, and no hook would let an extension do it outside core.
The GUC is off by default and the cost of the off path is one boolean check, so non-users pay little. The demand objection is a not-now point, not a rejection.
